c.tagline: Peru's City of Eternal Spring, ringed by adobe empires and surf-town sunsets.

taxi.fareNote: Most Trujillo taxis are unmetered; agree the fare before getting in, or use a ride app for a fixed price. Short trips in the center run a few soles.

emergency.note: 105 reaches the Peruvian National Police; 116 is the SAMU medical emergency line. 911 is not standard in Peru.

solo.f: Safety index is the main factor (42/100)

hood_desc: Trujillo's colonial core around the Plaza de Armas, full of pastel casonas, wrought-iron window grilles, churches, museums, restaurants and nightlife; the best base for first-timers who want everything walkable.

A laid-back Pacific surf-and-fishing town about 12 km northwest, famous for its long promenade, ceviche shacks, reed caballitos de totora boats and a World Surfing Reserve; ideal for travelers who want beach time over city bustle.

A central, well-connected residential urbanization just off the main avenues, close to clinics, universities, shopping and mid-range hotels; a convenient, safer-feeling base a short ride from the historic center.

An upscale, leafy district of gated urbanizations like El Golf and California near the coast, with modern apartments, malls and the city's smartest hotels and restaurants; suits travelers wanting comfort and calm.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water; tap water is not reliably potable.

transit.hours: City micros and combis run roughly 5:30 AM to around 11:00 PM; late-night travel relies on taxis and ride apps.
transit.note: Trujillo has no metro or rail. Public transport is a dense web of privately-run micros (small buses) and combis (shared minibuses) that connect the center with Huanchaco, Chan Chan, Moche and the districts, supplemented by taxis and ride-hailing apps.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver or cobrador on board (roughly S/1-2 within the city, a little more to Huanchaco). There is no unified transit card. Keep small change handy.

food.name: Ceviche norteno
food.desc: Big cubes of Pacific fish cured in lime with red onion, aji limo and the local aji mochero, served with yuca, choclo and toasted corn; bolder than Lima ceviche.

places.name: La Cevicheria del Norte
places.note: Reference cevicheria supplied each dawn by local fishermen with the day catch.

places.name: Big Ben Huanchaco

places.name: Mar Picante

food.name: Cabrito a la nortena
food.desc: Young goat marinated in chicha de jora, coriander and aji, slow-stewed until it falls apart and served with canary beans and rice; Trujillo defining dish.

places.name: El Mochica
places.note: More than 40 years old; its cabrito with beans is a reference of Trujillo identity.

places.name: Estancia Muchik
places.note: Elegant room with traditional flavours; the roast cabrito is the standout.

places.name: El Celler de Cler

food.name: Shambar
food.desc: Trujillo Monday soup: wheat, chickpeas, beans and lentils simmered with smoked pork and ham, finished with toasted corn on top. Served Mondays only.

places.name: El Mochica

places.name: Mercado Central de Trujillo
places.note: Market food counters ladle shambar to office workers every Monday morning.

places.name: Mercado La Hermelinda
places.note: Huge working market where the Monday shambar is cheapest and most authentic.

food.name: Arroz con pato a la chiclayana
food.desc: Duck braised then cooked into rice stained deep green with coriander and dark beer or chicha de jora, a northern coast Sunday centrepiece.

places.name: El Mochica

places.name: Estancia Muchik

places.name: Big Ben Huanchaco

food.desc: Black clams from the mangroves served raw in their juice, and thin-sliced raw fish under a sauce of the fiercely aromatic local aji mochero chilli.

places.name: El Celler de Cler
places.note: Signature aji mochero tiradito, a modern take on Trujillo flavours.

places.name: Estancia Muchik

places.name: Mar Picante

food.name: King Kong and northern sweets
food.desc: Layers of thick biscuit sandwiched with manjarblanco, pineapple jam and peanut fudge; the outsized sweet of the Peruvian north, sold by the slab.

places.name: Mercado Central de Trujillo
places.note: Sweet stalls sell King Kong, alfajores and manjarblanco by weight.

places.name: Mercado La Hermelinda

landmarks: Chan Chan
The largest adobe city on Earth, capital of the Chimú empire, spreads UNESCO-listed friezes of fish, pelicans and waves across nine walled palace compounds.
Huaca de la Luna
This Moche temple pyramid stuns with tiered polychrome murals of the fanged god Ai Apaec, revealed layer by layer beneath Cerro Blanco.
Plaza de Armas and Freedom Monument
Peru's proudest colonial square bursts with canary-yellow and cobalt mansions around the soaring marble Monumento a la Libertad celebrating independence.
Huanchaco Beach
Fishermen still ride caballitos de totora reed boats through the surf at this laid-back beach town, a cradle of Peruvian surfing and ceviche.
Trujillo Cathedral
The lemon-yellow 17th-century cathedral on the Plaza de Armas pairs a luminous Baroque interior with a museum of colonial religious art.
Huaca del Arco Iris (Huaca del Dragón)
A restored Chimú temple in suburban La Esperanza displays enigmatic rainbow-and-dragon friezes rippling across its adobe ramparts.
Casa Urquiaga
This impeccably restored blue colonial mansion, now owned by Peru's central bank, preserves Bolívar's desk and gleaming period salons open free to visitors.
Casa de la Emancipación
Trujillo's independence from Spain was proclaimed in this landmark mansion in 1820; today it hosts art exhibitions amid elegant republican-era architecture.
Museo de Arqueología de la Universidad de Trujillo
Set in a handsome colonial casona, this museum surveys ten millennia of northern Peru's cultures, from Cupisnique ceramics to Moche masterpieces.
Palacio Iturregui
A neoclassical mansion built in 1842 by independence leader Juan Manuel Iturregui, its courtyard ringed by 36 slender columns and gilded ceiling moldings.

train.note: Peru has no national intercity passenger rail network and none at all on the north coast - the only trains in the country run in the Andes around Cusco and Puno. Travel is by coach or by air into Trujillo's airport.

intl.to: Guayaquil & Quito (Ecuador) - long-haul via the Tumbes border

bus.note: Coaches are the way to travel Peru's coast. Cruz del Sur, Oltursa (https://www.oltursa.pe/) and Movil Tours run from their own terminals rather than one central station, reaching Lima in about 9 hours, Chiclayo in 3 and Máncora in 8. The Ecuador services continue north from Tumbes and take a day or more - carry your passport. Local combis serve Huanchaco and the Chan Chan ruins.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry from Trujillo - the nearby port of Salaverry handles cargo and occasional cruise calls. The reed caballitos de totora at Huanchaco are fishing craft and a surfing curiosity rather than transport.

half.name: El Brujo and Museo Cao
half.blurb: North along the coast, the El Brujo complex guards the tattooed mummy of the Lady of Cao, a female Moche ruler who rewrote Peruvian history.

laundry.note: Attended lavanderia por kilo is standard; self-service scarce
